steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Atlanta GA. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $96,500. Additional income: $18,400 (photography, 3 clients), $2,650 from Barclays, $670 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 720 sq ft. Deductions: $3,200 student loan interest (Great Lakes, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Red Cross have receipt; $540 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — that’s a good amount of detail. I’ll summarize how each item is treated, give a recommendation about itemizing vs. the standard deduction, explain the home-office options, and list the forms you’ll likely need. I’ll also flag a few clarifying questions where I need more numbers to be precise.

Quick summary / headline recommendations
- Your photography income ($18,400) is self-employment income — report it on Schedule C; you’ll owe income tax plus self‑employment (SE) tax unless you have sufficient expenses to reduce net profit.
- The Barclays ($2,650) and Merrill Edge ($670) amounts look like interest — include them as investment income. Since total taxable interest > $1,500, you’ll need Schedule B.
- The home-office deduction is available (you said 120 sq ft exclusively). You can choose the simplified method ($5/sq ft = $600) or the regular method (a share of actual home expenses — in your case rent allocates to about $3,500/year), and the regular method looks likely to give a bigger deduction if you only consider rent.
- Student loan interest is an “above-the-line” adjustment (up to $2,500) but phases out with MAGI; with your reported income it’s likely you’re above the phaseout — you may not be able to claim it. See details below.
- Unreimbursed employee expenses for W-2 work are generally NOT deductible for most taxpayers after the 2018 rules change. If the $540 are business expenses related to your photography (self-employment), include them on Schedule C instead.
- Most likely you’ll take the standard deduction unless you have mortgage interest, large state/property taxes, or more charitable contributions than you noted. Based on the numbers you gave, standard deduction will probably be larger — see the comparison section below.

Details and calculations (using the numbers you gave)
1) Self-employment (photography) — what you must do
- Report all gross receipts on Schedule C (Form 1040). That includes the $18,400 from the 3 clients even if you didn’t receive 1099s.
- Deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses on Schedule C (supplies, equipment, business insurance, advertising, home office, mileage, etc.). If the $540 you listed are business expenses, treat them on Schedule C.
- You will owe self-employment tax (Schedule SE) on net earnings from self-employment (net = gross receipts − business expenses). SE tax is roughly 15.3% on net earnings (after the 7.65% adjustment), and you get an “above-the-line” deduction for one-half of your SE tax.

Example (rough) using only the items you listed and assuming the $540 is a business expense:
- Gross self-employment income: $18,400
- Home-office deduction (regular method using rent allocation — see below): about $3,500
- Other expenses: $540
- Net profit ≈ $18,400 − $3,500 − $540 = $14,360
- Net earnings subject to SE tax ≈ 14,360 × 0.9235 ≈ 13,265
- SE tax ≈ 13,265 × 15.3% ≈ $2,028 (half, ~$1,014, is deductible on Schedule 1)

(These are illustrative; actual tax numbers will vary slightly with exact formulas.)

2) Home office (you asked how to treat it)
You gave: home = 720 sq ft; home office = 120 sq ft exclusive; rent = $1,750/month → annual rent = $21,000.
- Office percentage = 120 / 720 = 16.6667% (1/6).
- Regular method: allocate actual home expenses to business. With just rent, the home-office portion = 16.6667% × $21,000 = $3,500. If you also have utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., a proportionate share of those is deductible too (and depreciation if you own). To use the regular method for a sole proprietor you complete Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home), and some depreciation or carryforward rules may apply.
- Simplified method: $5 × 120 sq ft = $600 (no Form 8829, just enter on Schedule C).
- Recommendation: based on rent only, the regular method ($3,500) beats the simplified ($600). Use the regular method if you can document rent, utilities, etc. Note: the home-office deduction cannot exceed net profit from your business. If it would, the excess may be carried forward.

3) Interest income (Barclays + Merrill Edge)
- Total interest $2,650 + $670 = $3,320. Report on Form 1040; because taxable interest > $1,500, attach Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends).
- If Merrill Edge generated dividends, stock sales, or capital gains, you may also need Form 8949 / Schedule D — confirm whether the $670 was interest, dividend, or sale proceeds (look at the 1099(s) you received).

4) Student loan interest ($3,200 note)
- The student loan interest deduction (up to $2,500) is an adjustment to income (reported on Schedule 1) and phases out based on modified adjusted gross income (MAGI).
- In recent years for single filers the phaseout range started in the mid-to-high $70k range and phased out by the low $90k range (the exact thresholds change yearly). With W‑2 wages of $96,500 plus ~ $14k net self‑employment income (per example), your MAGI is likely above the allowable limit, so you probably won’t be eligible for the student loan interest deduction. If the $3,200 you listed is interest paid in prior years or not paid in the calendar year, only interest paid in the tax year counts. Check the Form 1098-E from your servicer (Great Lakes) for the exact amount paid in the tax year; if it is >0 and your MAGI is under the phaseout upper limit you can claim up to $2,500.
- Action: confirm the amount of interest actually paid in the tax year (1098-E) and compute MAGI to see if you fall under the phaseout.

5) Charitable contributions ($1,500)
- Deductible only if you itemize. If you take the standard deduction, you cannot separately deduct these contributions on your federal return (except rare above-the-line provisions that do not apply generally for 2024).
- Keep the receipt you mentioned (good documentation).

6) Unreimbursed expenses ($540)
- If these are unreimbursed employee expenses related to your W‑2 job: generally not deductible for most taxpayers under the post‑2018 rules (except certain categories like reservists, qualified performing artists, etc.). So likely not deductible.
- If they are business expenses related to photography (self-employed), include them on Schedule C.

7) Itemize vs. standard deduction
- To decide, add up your potential itemized deductions:
  - Charitable contributions: $1,500
  - State and local taxes (SALT): state income tax + property tax, capped at $10,000 total (federal cap)
  - Mortgage interest (if any) and medical expense amounts that exceed the applicable AGI threshold (if any)
- If your SALT + charity + mortgage interest (if any) exceed the standard deduction for a single filer for tax year 2024, itemize; otherwise take the standard deduction.
- Based on the numbers you gave (only $1,500 charity and no mortgage interest or property tax numbers), you’ll most likely be better off taking the standard deduction — especially because SALT is capped at $10,000 and you didn’t list large property taxes or mortgage interest. If you do have mortgage interest or significant property taxes, that could change the outcome.

(If you want, provide how much Georgia state income tax was withheld or property tax paid and I’ll compute a direct comparison.)

8) Forms you will likely need
- Form 1040 (U.S. Individual Income Tax Return).
- Schedule 1 (Additional Income and Adjustments) — for adjustments such as student loan interest (if allowed) and the deduction for half of SE tax.
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — to report photography income and related business expenses.
- Schedule SE (Self-Employment Tax) — to compute SE tax.
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if you use the regular home-office method.
- Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends) — because your taxable interest exceeds $1,500.
- Possibly Form 4562 (Depreciation) — if you’re depreciating business equipment or part of the home under the regular method.
- State tax return — Georgia Form 500 (or whatever Georgia requires).
- Keep Forms 1099-NEC / 1099-MISC from clients (if any), 1099-INT, 1099-DIV, 1099-B, and 1098-E (student loan interest) for your records.

9) Recordkeeping and other tips
- Keep receipts and a log for home-office exclusive use, utilities, rent receipts, business receipts, mileage log, and charitable receipts.
- Make sure the student loan interest amount you claim matches Form 1098‑E from Great Lakes for the tax year.
- If you expect to owe tax after considering withholding and SE tax, consider making estimated tax payments (quarterly) or increasing W‑2 withholding to avoid penalties.
- If you haven’t already, gather your W‑2, all 1099s, 1098‑E, and any brokerage statements before preparing the return.

Clarifying questions (so I can give a precise recommendation)
1. Is the $3,200 in student loan interest the amount actually paid in the most recent tax year (i.e., 2024)? Do you have a 1098‑E showing that amount for the tax year you are filing?
2. Are the $540 unreimbursed expenses related to your photography business (self‑employment) or to your W‑2 job?
3. Do you have mortgage interest or property tax amounts for 2024? Do you know how much Georgia state tax was withheld or how much state income tax you paid in 2024?
4. Were the Barclays/Merrill amounts interest (1099‑INT) or something else (dividends, capital gains)?

If you want, give me the answers to those questions and I’ll:
- run the numbers to show expected federal tax, SE tax, and whether you should itemize or take the standard deduction; and
- recommend whether the regular or simplified home‑office method is better once I have any other home expenses or utility numbers.

Would you like me to do a sample tax calculation (estimate) using the assumptions above, or would you prefer I first get the clarifying details?
